sections.title: Computer vision AI in 2026: The state of the art
sections.description: The computer vision AI landscape has transformed dramatically since 2020. Foundation models, transformer-based detection, vision-language models, and efficient edge deployment have elevated the performance ceiling dramatically.

blocks.heading: Key advances driving CV today
paragraphs: Foundation vision models (CLIP, Segment Anything Model/SAM, DINOv2, Florence) provide rich visual representations without task-specific training data. Transformer-based detection architectures (DETR, DINO, RT-DETR) outperform CNN-based detectors on many benchmarks. Vision-Language Models (GPT-4 Vision, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, LLaVA) enable natural language interaction with visual content. Efficient edge deployment (YOLOv8/v9/v10, MobileNetV3, EfficientDet) runs inference on embedded hardware at real-time speeds.
A CV model that required 50,000 labeled images to train adequately in 2019 may now be achievable with 2,000 labeled images through transfer learning from foundation models.
ClickMasters keeps pace with this rapidly evolving landscape. We recommend the current state-of-the-art approach for each use case — not the approach we built capability in three years ago.

sections.title: Computer vision data requirements and labeling
sections.description: Every supervised CV model requires labeled training data. The volume depends on model architecture, transfer learning approach, and task complexity.

blocks.heading: Label volume estimates
paragraphs: Image classification (transfer learning from foundation model): 200–2,000 images per class.
Object detection (fine-tuning YOLO or DETR): 500–5,000 annotated examples.
Medical imaging (disease classification): 1,000–50,000 cases with clinical labels.
Anomaly detection (normal examples only): 100–2,000 defect-free images.

blocks.heading: Labeling tools and services
paragraphs: ClickMasters uses Label Studio (open-source), Roboflow (commercial, with active learning), and Scale AI (enterprise labeling service) for annotation. For medical imaging, clinical annotation requires credentialed annotators (radiologists, pathologists) — ClickMasters sources clinical annotation through established annotation services with the appropriate clinical credentials.

blocks.heading: Active learning to reduce labeling cost
paragraphs: Active learning — training an initial model on a small labeled set, then using the model to identify which unlabeled images would be most informative to label next — typically reduces total labeling requirements by 30–60% compared to random sampling. ClickMasters implements active learning loops for all CV engagements where labeling is a significant cost driver.

items.question: What is the best object detection model in 2026?
items.answer: For real-time inference at edge (embedded GPU): YOLOv9 or YOLOv10 — best accuracy/speed trade-off for most industrial applications. For highest accuracy (server-side inference): RT-DETR (Real-Time DEtection Transformer) or DINO. For open-set detection (detecting objects not in training data): Grounding DINO with open-vocabulary detection. ClickMasters recommends based on your latency, throughput, and accuracy requirements.

items.question: How much labeled training data does a computer vision model require?
items.answer: With transfer learning from foundation models (CLIP, DINOv2, SAM): 200–2,000 labeled examples per class for classification; 500–5,000 for detection. Without transfer learning: 5–50× more. Active learning reduces total labeling requirements by 30–60%. ClickMasters assesses labeling requirements during Discovery and includes labeling cost in the total project estimate.

items.question: Can computer vision replace human quality inspectors?
items.answer: CV achieves better than human accuracy on structured defect detection tasks in controlled lighting conditions — typically 97–99.5% accuracy vs. human inspector accuracy of 80–95% at production speeds. CV is most appropriate as a 100% automated screening layer with human review of flagged items. Complete replacement of human inspectors depends on the defect type, lighting control, and regulatory requirements of your specific application.

items.question: What are the FDA requirements for medical imaging AI?
items.answer: Most medical imaging AI that assists clinical diagnosis is classified as Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and requires FDA clearance. The pathway (510(k), De Novo, or PMA) depends on the intended use and risk level. ClickMasters advises on FDA SaMD classification during Discovery and designs the clinical validation study the FDA submission requires.

items.question: How long does computer vision development take?
items.answer: Image classification: 10–16 weeks. Object detection: 12–20 weeks. Segmentation and pose estimation: 14–22 weeks. Medical imaging AI: 16–32 weeks. Video analytics: 14–24 weeks. 3D point cloud: 16–28 weeks. Timeline is contractually binding from Discovery.
